trial_name: REVISE — Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis during Invasive Mechanical Ventilation (2024)
citation: Cook D, Deane A, Lauzier F, Zytaruk N, Guyatt G, Saunders L, et al; REVISE Investigators. Stress ulcer prophylaxis during invasive mechanical ventilation. N Engl J Med. 2024 Jul 4;391(1):9-20.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, pragmatic
one_liner: Pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper GI bleeding (1.0% vs 3.5%, HR 0.30) without increasing 90-day mortality (29.1% vs 30.9%, HR 0.94) in ventilated ICU adults.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in ICU, expected to remain ventilated beyond the calendar day after randomisation, without strong indication for acid suppression or high bleeding risk antithrombotic regimens.
pico.intervention: Pantoprazole 40 mg IV once daily while invasively ventilated.
pico.outcome: Primary efficacy: clinically important upper GI bleeding; primary safety: 90-day all-cause mortality.

background.existing_knowledge: Stress-related mucosal disease can cause upper GI bleeding in critical illness; incidence has fallen with modern ICU practices. Acid suppression reduces bleeding but may increase infections. Prior RCTs showed pantoprazole reduced bleeding but mortality and infectious harms uncertain.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether pantoprazole reduces clinically important bleeding and affects mortality in contemporary ventilated ICU patients.
background.hypothesis: Pantoprazole would reduce clinically important upper GI bleeding without increasing 90-day mortality.

methods.design: International, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group pragmatic trial in 68 ICUs across 8 countries.
methods.setting: 68 ICUs, 8 countries; enrollment dates not reported.

inclusion: Adults ≥18 years receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, expected to remain ventilated beyond the calendar day after randomisation.
exclusion: Invasive mechanical ventilation >72 hours during admission
Active GI bleeding or high-risk bleeding indication requiring acid suppression
Receipt in ICU of >1 daily dose equivalent of PPI or H2RA
Palliative care/anticipated withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy

methods.intervention: Pantoprazole 40 mg IV once daily, started soon after randomisation, continued while invasively ventilated in ICU.
methods.comparison: Matching placebo IV once daily, same administration and stopping rules.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (participants, clinicians, research staff, adjudicators, analysts).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 4,800 to detect 1.5 percentage point absolute reduction in clinically important bleeding (3.0% to 1.5%) with 85% power at two-sided 5% significance.
methods.primary_outcome: Primary efficacy: clinically important upper GI bleeding; primary safety: 90-day all-cause mortality.
secondary_outcomes: Initiation of renal replacement therapy in ICU
Total units of red blood cells transfused in ICU
methods.follow_up: 90 days for mortality; in-ICU for bleeding and several secondary endpoints.

headline_bullets: Pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper GI bleeding from 3.5% to 1.0% (HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.19–0.47, P<0.001).
90-day mortality was similar: 29.1% vs 30.9% (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85–1.04, P=0.25).
Patient-important bleeding also reduced (1.5% vs 4.2%, HR 0.36).
No significant differences in ventilator-associated pneumonia, RRT initiation, or other secondary outcomes; C. difficile numerically higher but inconclusive.

outcomes_table.outcome: Clinically important upper GI bleeding (primary efficacy)
outcomes_table.note: Absolute difference 2.5 percentage points (95% CI 1.6 to 3.3)
Adjusted for baseline APACHE II score
Multiplicity-adjusted p value; low event counts

outcomes_table.outcome: Total RBC units transfused in ICU (tertiary)
outcomes_table.note: Negative binomial model; multiplicity-adjusted p value

outcomes_table.outcome: Peak serum creatinine in ICU, mg/dL (tertiary)
Duration of invasive mechanical ventilation, days (tertiary)

safety: No significant differences in other safety outcomes; open-label acid suppression use was low (4.4% vs 5.4% PPI, 0.8% vs 1.3% H2RA).

domains.notes: Central web-based 1:1 randomisation with allocation concealment, stratified by centre and pre-hospital acid suppression; variable block sizes.
Double-blind, masking extended to all parties; no unblinding requests.
79 (1.6%) excluded post-randomisation (consent withdrawal/ineligible); 98.9% vital status at 90 days.
Study drug started within 24h in >92%; median 86.7% vs 84.6% of ventilator days; open-label PPI use 4.4% vs 5.4%.
Well balanced: mean age ~58, APACHE II 21.7, similar pre-hospital acid suppression, anticoagulation, enteral nutrition.

internal_validity.verdict: Strong internal validity: robust randomisation, blinding, adherence, and follow-up; minor post-randomisation exclusions and limited precision for rare harms.

domains.notes: Broad adult ventilated ICU population across 8 countries, moderate-to-high acuity (mean APACHE II ~22), common diagnoses.

Applies to ventilated ICU adults without strong acid suppression indication or dual antiplatelet/therapeutic anticoagulation; less applicable where IV PPI supply or infection diagnostics limited; absolute benefit varies with baseline bleeding risk.

external_validity.verdict: High generalisability for contemporary ventilated ICU practice in similar health systems; limited for populations with mandated acid suppression or markedly different bleeding risk.

strengths: Large, international, double-blind, placebo-controlled design with pragmatic delivery.
Dual primary endpoints addressing efficacy and safety.
Clinically and patient-centred bleeding outcomes with concordant benefit.
High follow-up and prespecified multiplicity handling.
limitations: Post-randomisation exclusions led to modified ITT analysis.
Rare harms (C. difficile) had low event counts and wide confidence intervals.
VAP definition used CPIS score, less objective than microbiology-confirmed.
Findings less applicable to patients with strong acid-suppression indications or higher bleeding-risk antithrombotic regimens.

critical_appraisal.summary: REVISE provides high-certainty evidence that pantoprazole reduces clinically important GI bleeding without increasing mortality in ventilated ICU adults, with strong internal validity; uncertainty remains for rare infectious harms.
strengths: High protocol adherence and low crossover
Prespecified dual primary endpoints and multiplicity adjustment
weaknesses: Modified ITT due to post-randomisation exclusions
Imprecise estimates for rare harms like C. difficile

sections.authors_conclusion: Among invasively mechanically ventilated ICU adults, pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding compared with placebo, with no significant difference in 90-day mortality.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Pantoprazole should be used for stress ulcer prophylaxis in ventilated ICU adults without contraindications, as it reduces clinically important bleeding without increasing mortality; however, the absolute benefit is modest and risk of rare harms remains uncertain, so prophylaxis should be stopped when ventilation ceases and bleeding risk resolves.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, without strong indication for acid suppression or high bleeding risk antithrombotic regimens.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Pantoprazole does not reduce mortality or duration of ventilation; it is not a substitute for early enteral nutrition or other bleeding prevention measures.
implementation_caveats: Discontinue when extubated and bleeding risk factors resolve.
Avoid in patients with dual antiplatelet therapy or combined antiplatelet plus therapeutic anticoagulation (excluded from trial).
Monitor for C. difficile, though absolute risk increase is small and uncertain.

controversies.topic: Composite endpoint and dual primary design
controversies.notes: REVISE used dual primary endpoints (efficacy and safety) to address both benefit and harm, strengthening interpretability.
Guidelines and editorial emphasize targeting prophylaxis to higher-risk patients and stopping when risk abates, rather than routine universal use.
C. difficile and other infections remain imprecisely estimated; net benefit may be smaller in low-risk populations.
Prior PEPTIC trial did not show clear mortality difference between PPIs and H2RAs; REVISE does not directly compare classes but supports PPI efficacy vs placebo.

context_related_trials.relation: Earlier placebo-controlled trial of pantoprazole in ICU patients, showed reduced GI bleeding but uncertain mortality effect; REVISE confirms and extends with larger sample and dual primary endpoints.
Large cluster crossover trial comparing PPIs vs H2RAs in ICU, found no mortality difference; REVISE provides placebo-controlled evidence for PPI efficacy.

unresolved_questions: Optimal duration of prophylaxis and criteria for discontinuation.
Net benefit in patients with very low baseline bleeding risk.
Comparative effectiveness of PPIs vs H2RAs for mortality and rare harms.
Effect in patients with dual antiplatelet or combined antithrombotic therapy.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In ventilated ICU adults, pantoprazole reduces clinically important GI bleeding without increasing mortality, supporting targeted prophylaxis with prompt discontinuation when risk resolves.
